vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus sits in the waiting room of the clinic with his hands folded in his lap, his wedding ring catching the fluorescent light. At fifty-four, he carries himself with the careful posture of someone who has spent thirty years in law enforcement—shoulders back, chin level, always aware of exits and potential threats. His parole officer badge rests on his belt, though today he's taken leave from work. This is his third session.

He describes the incident with precision, as if reciting facts from a case file. Eighteen months ago, he responded to a domestic disturbance call in a neighborhood where he'd grown up. The call came in around midnight. When Marcus and his partner arrived, they found a man—someone Marcus had actually supervised years earlier on parole—standing in the street with a knife. Marcus knew this man. He'd seen his parenting struggles, his efforts to stay clean, his small victories. He'd believed in his rehabilitation.

What should have been a routine call went wrong in seconds. The man lunged. Marcus's partner, a younger officer Marcus had trained, panicked and opened fire. Marcus watched his former parolee collapse on the asphalt of a street he'd walked as a boy. The man survived but was permanently disabled. Marcus was cleared of wrongdoing—he hadn't fired his weapon—but something fractured inside him that night.

He stopped sleeping well around six months after. At first, it was just the occasional night where he'd wake at 2 a.m., his heart racing, convinced he was back on that street. His wife, Rosa, would find him in the kitchen at three in the morning, drinking coffee and staring at nothing. Now, most nights are like that. He lies beside her, hypervigilant, listening to the neighborhood sounds he's never noticed before—the distant sirens, the wind against the gutters, the creak of the house settling.

Work became increasingly difficult. The job that had defined him for three decades now triggers an almost unbearable anxiety. When he's with parolees, he finds himself catastrophizing—imagining worst-case scenarios, seeing danger where none exists. He's become overprotective, almost rigid in his enforcement. Two months ago, he wrote up a young man for a minor parole violation that he would have overlooked years before. The guilt afterward kept him awake for a week. He's started questioning whether he's still capable of doing this work fairly, whether his judgment has been compromised.

His concentration has deteriorated. Reports that once took him an hour now take three. Rosa mentions that he seems distant, that he doesn't laugh anymore. He's withdrawn from his regular poker games with friends, from the community center where he used to volunteer. When his grandchildren visit, he finds himself irritable, snapping at them over small things, then feeling a crushing remorse that exhausts him further.

The worst moments come unexpectedly. A car backfires on his commute and his entire body goes rigid. He finds himself replaying the scene obsessively—not what happened, but what could have happened. What if his partner hadn't been there? What if Marcus had been the one holding the gun? He knows intellectually that he did nothing wrong, that he followed protocol, that the outcome wasn't his fault. But his body doesn't believe his mind.

Marcus has always been someone who solved problems, who protected others, who maintained control. Now he feels like a passenger in his own life, watching himself deteriorate and unable to stop it. The badge that once brought him pride now feels like an accusation.
